, in general, the northern Sierra Madres Occidental and southwestern United States were affected by similar tectonic and magmatic processes during the mid-Tertiary, but the timing and details of these processes were different.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the evolution of subduction-related magmas in the northern Sierra is similar to that of magmas in the Basin and Range province, but that the two provinces are separated by the Mojave-Sonora megashear.

the evolution of magmatism and the onset of crust extension in both areas were driven by a common geologic process, namely, a change in the rate of convergence between the North America and Farallon plates.
the evolution of waned subduction-related magmas in the northern Sierra is broadly comparable to that observed in the southwestern United States.
The main takeaway from our work is that

, in both the northern Sierra Madren Occidental and the southwestern United States, the evolution of waneing, subduction-related activity was characterized by a decrease in the flux of mafics from the mantle, the stagnation and differentiation of intermediate-composition magma bodies, and the onset of crust extension.
the evolution of magmatism in a subduction-related setting is not always a simple function of the rate of plate convergence.
